garish

/GAIR-ish/ - the stress falls on GAIR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Garish means gaudy — loud, clashing show in bad taste.

The stadium's new scoreboard felt garish in the century-old park, all strobing red against brick and ivy.

Worked Example

The landlord repainted the hallway in traffic-cone orange with mint-green trim, a combination so garish that tenants joked about needing sunglasses to collect the mail.

Garish is the right word because the colors don't just stand out — they clash, shout, and offend the eye. Bold color used well is striking; color this loud and this graceless is garish, and the word passes judgment as it describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

gaudy: Gaudy is the closest cousin — flashy, cheap-looking display, colors and glitter chosen to impress and failing. Garish adds assault: the colors don't just look cheap, they clash and shout until the eye actually winces. Gaudy misjudges taste; garish attacks it.

tawdry: Tawdry is showy on top and shabby underneath — thin glitter with cheapness showing through it. Garish is about the visual assault itself: loud, clashing color in bad taste, however much it cost. A garish ballroom can cost millions; tawdry always smells of cheapness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tasteful: quietly well-chosen

subdued: softened and toned down

Where it sits · how hard it grabs at the eye — bold → flashy → garish

bold vs. garish: Bold is confident color that stops far short of garish — assured, not assaulting.

flashy vs. garish: Flashy goes further than bold — it wants your attention — but stops short of garish, which crosses into eyesore.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — garish

Root — garish: whole word of uncertain origin, possibly from Middle English gauren, to stare

Put it together

Put it together: Garish resists dissection: there is no prefix or suffix to peel, and its origin is genuinely uncertain. The best guess ties it to Middle English gauren, 'to stare' — fitting, since a garish thing is exactly what makes everyone stare, and wince.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Because garish's ancestry is disputed — the staring-word gauren is only a likely parent, and that verb itself died out — no confirmed relatives survive in modern English. The word stands alone, as loud in the dictionary as the colors it describes.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral, disapproving

Garish condemns loud, clashing visual taste — neon on brick, sequins at a funeral. Keep it apart from two neighbors in this unit: ornate measures how much decoration there is without necessarily disapproving, and lurid does for content what garish does for color — a poster's colors are garish, its gory details are lurid.
